title: 9. Bull vs. Bear, Portfolio Action & Redeployment Plan
web_title: 9. Bull vs. Bear, Portfolio Action & Redeployment Plan
book_title: Chapter 9: Bull vs. Bear, Likely Outcomes & Our Action Plan
question: If you set the strongest case for Creative Newtech beside the strongest case against it, which side does the evidence favour at ₹1,458.40, and what should you do with new money?

epigraph.quote: In the short run, the market is a voting machine, but in the long run it is a weighing machine.
epigraph.author: Benjamin Graham, as quoted by Warren Buffett in the 1993 Berkshire Hathaway letter

web_blocks.text: Chapters 1 to 6 established the business without reference to any price: a profitable, fast-growing technology distributor with a high-margin brand franchise inside it, thin cash conversion, and a funding model that leans on suppliers, banks and customer advances. Chapters 7 and 8 then priced it and read the tape. This chapter puts the best argument for the stock beside the best argument against it, weights them with explicit probabilities, and converts the result into a decision for new capital, a statement about the current holding (none), and a destination for the money. The rule we apply is the same for every name: a non-rejected call needs the base-case value to sit above the top of the support zone with at least 1.5 units of reward for every unit of risk. [30][31][57]

web_blocks.title: The Institutional Bull Case (Steelmanned)
paragraphs: 1. The earnings engine is real and audited. Total income rose from ₹370.70 Cr in FY19 to ₹2,717.51 Cr in FY26, a 33% annual rate, while attributable EPS grew from ₹5.04 to ₹41.20, a 35% rate. H1 FY27 profit after tax rose 35.5% on 16.6% revenue growth because EBITDA margin widened to 5.28% from 3.95%. Profit is converting faster than sales, which is what operating leverage looks like. [29][33]

2. The mix is moving toward the part of the business that earns real margin. Brand Business was 14.1% of FY26 revenue, 17.4% in H1 FY27 and 19.0% in Q2 FY27, and it earned a 33.2% segment margin against 3.8% for Market Entry in FY26. Gross margin printed 11.34% in Q2 FY27 against 7.90% a year earlier. If brand share reaches 25%, blended margins rise without any new rupee of distribution volume. [30][33]

3. The balance sheet has just been repaired. Borrowings fell from ₹324 Cr in March 2026 to ₹194 Cr in September 2026, the company reported net cash of about ₹30 Cr, operating cash flow for H1 FY27 was +₹351.24 Cr, and interest cover is about 5x against a Crisil trigger of 3x. The rating agency reaffirmed BBB+/Stable in August 2026. [31][39]

4. The runway has several independent legs. Surveillance (Matrix, Sparsh, the proposed Infinova and Zicom SaaS acquisitions), data-centre cabling through Honeywell, the WOZOYO own brand, drones, and a conditional ₹3,194.83 Cr BharatNet consortium order each give Creative a path to growth that does not depend on the other four. Management has framed a ₹6,000 Cr FY29 revenue ambition and a 40% brand share. [32][33][11]

5. Management does what it can book. Four of the fifteen commitments scored in Chapter 5 were delivered in full, all of them 12-month revenue, brand or profit figures, and the company is now a listed, rated, BSE-and-NSE-traded business with 10,000+ channel partners and 18 warehouses. [34][15]

6. The market is already voting for it. The stock is in a Stage 2 uptrend, it is up 176% since 31 March 2026, and its relative strength is the highest in its peer set, with Redington, Rashi Peripherals and CP Plus all weaker over one month. Momentum has a habit of persisting longer than sceptics expect. [57][58]

web_blocks.title: The Institutional Bear & Skeptic Case (Steelmanned)
paragraphs: 1. The price already assumes the good outcome. At ₹1,458.40 the stock trades at 30.7x trailing attributable EPS of ₹47.44 and 5.46x book value, against 13.6x for Redington and 11.9x for Rashi Peripherals. On 31 March 2026 the multiple was 12.9x. Since then the price has risen 2.76x while trailing EPS rose only 15.6%, so the multiple itself expanded 2.4x and most of the gain is re-rating, not earnings. [29][57]

2. Profit has not yet become cash. Operating cash flow was negative in seven of eight years, a cumulative −₹328 Cr against ₹241 Cr of profit. About 84% of the H1 FY27 inflow of ₹351.24 Cr came from a net release of working capital, led by payables and other liabilities, and the CFO told investors on the 29 October 2026 call that 45 net working capital days is not sustainable and that the normal range is 52 to 55 days. [30][31][32]

3. A single licence carries about half of EBITDA. Honeywell supplied ₹369.61 Cr of brand revenue, renewal falls in March 2027, management has described the term in several different ways, the royalty was only ₹5.96 Cr (1.6% of sales) and therefore has room to be reset upward, and the licensor is being split into separate companies. The largest customer is about 25% of revenue. [15][16][39]

4. The track record is better on sales than on cash. Four of fifteen commitments were delivered, all of them 12-month revenue, brand or profit figures; none of the four cash or working-capital promises was met. The ₹6,000 Cr FY29 target needs the brand business to compound at roughly 85% a year, and we put the chance of reaching it near one in four. [34][33]

5. Funding needs and dilution risk are rising. The board has approved the Zicom SaaS purchase at an enterprise value of ₹50.50 Cr, ₹25.50 Cr of it by issuing 2,25,000 new shares on a preferential basis (about 1.5% dilution), a ₹25 Cr cash payment, a new Singapore subsidiary, and a shareholder meeting on 28 November 2026. The CMD told the October call that a larger acquisition would mean raising capital "for sure." Secure Connection earns 53% of consolidated profit under separate auditors, and a ₹47.74 Cr related-party balance with Click Retail exceeds the note's related-party receivables total. [55][56][32][30]

6. The tape is stretched and thin. The stock is 21.3% above its 10-week EMA, 25.7% above its 50-DMA and 52.1% above its 30-week SMA, with RSI of 67.1 daily and 73.0 weekly. The last session traded only 14,339 shares, 0.36x the 30-day average, the average daily turnover is about ₹5.8 Cr, and NSE lists the stock under the long-term additional surveillance measure, stage II. A fast exit is not guaranteed if sentiment turns. [57][58]

web_blocks.text: Weighing the two sides, we find the Bull case stronger as an account of the business and the Bear case stronger as an account of the price. The Bull points are mostly facts already in the audited record: growth, mix, a repaired balance sheet. The Bear points are partly facts (the multiple, the cash history, the licence) and partly dated risks that fall inside the next five months: the 28 November meeting, the Q3 festive quarter results due in February 2027, and the Honeywell renewal in March 2027. The decisive asymmetry is that good news on each of these is substantially priced in, because the multiple has already re-rated by 2.4x, while bad news is not. We therefore weight the outcomes as follows. [31][32][57]

web_blocks.caption: Probability-weighted 12-month scenario analysis for Creative Newtech Limited (CMP ₹1,458.40; FY28E EPS is attributable to owners after an 11.5% minority share)
rows: H2 FY27 revenue +26%, FY28 +30%; EBITDA margin 5.00% in H2 FY27 and 5.25% in FY28; net working capital holds near 50 days; brand share passes 20%; Honeywell renews on broadly current terms; no further equity raise.

H2 FY27 revenue +15%, FY28 +24%; EBITDA margin 4.40% then 4.55%; working capital drifts to 52 to 55 days and interest rises to about ₹44 Cr; Honeywell renews with a higher minimum guarantee; Zicom and Infinova integrate without loss.

H2 FY27 revenue +8%, FY28 +8%; margin 3.90% then 3.80%; the H1 FY27 payables and advances partly unwind, interest reaches about ₹52 Cr; a licence reset or vendor loss trims brand profit; one more equity raise.
web_blocks.takeaway: Probability-weighted value is ₹1,287.12 per share, 11.7% below the ₹1,458.40 close. The base case alone is 7.3% below it. The 12-month expected return is roughly 24 percentage points short of the 12% annual hurdle we require for an equity with this cash-flow record. [30][31][32]

web_blocks.takeaway: Even a pullback into the technical support band fails the 1.5 : 1 test by a wide margin, because the base-case value is only 4.2% above the top of that band. A price near ₹1,089 or lower would be needed on today's evidence, and only if the funding-quality questions in Chapters 5 and 6 improve. [57]

web_blocks.text: This sizing table is a monitoring reference, not an order. Because the call for new capital is REJECTED, the risk-unit allocation is zero until the evidence changes; the levels are shown so you can see exactly where the structure would be defended if a position were ever authorised.

Three-horizon judgment. Short term (0 to 3 months, trading and momentum): NEUTRAL, no edge at the current price. The Stage 2 trend is genuine, but the stock is 21.3% above its 10-week EMA after a 36% one-month move, volume is drying up as the price rises, and the technical timing gate reads CAP_WAIT_FOR_SUPPORT. A tactical buyer would have a better entry in the ₹1,202 to ₹1,298 band after a contracting-volume pullback, but even that entry carries only 0.14 : 1 on our base case, so we do not treat it as a trade. Medium term (3 to 18 months): NO ALLOCATION. The probability-weighted outcome is −11.7%, and the dated catalysts (the 28 November shareholder meeting, Q3 FY27 results in February 2027, the Honeywell renewal in March 2027) are mostly asymmetric to the downside at a 30.7x multiple. Long term (3 to 5 years): CONDITIONAL, not a stay-away. If management delivers our probability-weighted FY29 revenue of about ₹5,280 Cr at a 4.55% EBITDA margin, FY29 EPS is about ₹89 and a 20x multiple gives about ₹1,785, a return of roughly 7% a year from today; it takes either a 5% margin or a 25x multiple to clear 12% a year, and management's own ₹6,000 Cr plan at a 5.25% margin would give about ₹2,525, roughly 20% a year. That outcome has roughly a one-in-four chance, so the long-term case is real but not yet a case for paying today's price. [30][33][32]

Evidence-first dual verdict and portfolio action. (1) New-capital verdict: REJECTED. The business-quality verdict is CYCLICAL_CONDITIONAL, which allows a purchase only where the price pays for the conditionality. At ₹1,458.40 it does not: the base-case value is below the price, the probability-weighted value is 11.7% below it, and the support-zone asymmetry of 0.14 : 1 is far below the 1.5 : 1 hurdle. We reject rather than hedge with WAIT_FOR_SUPPORT, because waiting for the technical support band does not repair the reward-to-risk; only a lower price or better cash evidence does. (2) Current holding action: NOT_HELD. The same-session positions ledger shows no CNL shares in any account, so there is nothing to hold, trim or exit, and zero shares are recommended for sale. The alerts below are advisory and are not broker orders. [57]

Redeployment plan. Because CNL is not held, the capital under review is the next marginal unit of cash, and we allocate 100% of it to cash. We compared it with the active shortlist and with researched outside names. Among shortlist names, AJMERA (close ₹133.28) and MANORAMA (close ₹1,984.10) are each already 4% of net worth and carry favourable evidence records in their own dossiers, but both closed above the top of their published support bands (₹132.17 and ₹1,957.58), and neither was re-underwritten in this run, so a cross-name transfer from this report is not warranted; each is a candidate for its own refresh. Among outside names, Redington (close ₹349.70, 13.6x trailing earnings, 31% revenue growth) sits in Stage 3 below its 50-day average, and our derived base value of ₹403 (14x a forward EPS of ₹28.80) gives 0.82 : 1 at the close. Rashi Peripherals is in a downtrend, 22% lower in a month. Cash earns a positive carry while we wait, whereas a negative expected return does not. [57]

Execution triggers for a future re-underwrite of CNL: (a) a price at or below ₹1,089 with the stop at ₹913.79, which is where the base case clears 1.5 : 1; (b) the Q3 FY27 results (due February 2027) showing net working capital between 52 and 55 days while cumulative nine-month operating cash flow remains at least 50% of profit, so that the H1 payables inflow proves structural; (c) written clarity on the Honeywell renewal terms due in March 2027; and (d) the 28 November 2026 shareholder vote and the final preferential price for the Zicom SaaS shares disclosed without a larger equity raise. A weekly close above ₹1,550.20 on volume above 1.5x the 30-day average would refresh the momentum read but would not by itself change the REJECTED call.

book_paragraphs: Let me ask you to hold two pictures in your head at once, because everything in this chapter depends on keeping them apart. The first picture is a company: a Mumbai distributor that has compounded revenue at 33% a year for seven years, grown its profit more than twelve-fold, and just printed the best margin quarter in its history. The second picture is a share price: ₹1,458.40, up from ₹528.15 on the last day of March. Most investors blur the two. The company is good, so the stock must be good. This chapter is where you and I refuse to blur them, because a company can be worth owning and a stock can still be worth declining.

Start with the best case for owning it, and let me argue it as hard as its smartest supporter would. Profit is audited, and it is growing faster than sales. Brand Business, the licensed-and-owned half of the story, was 14% of revenue last year and 19% last quarter, and it earns around a third of its revenue as segment profit while the distribution road earns under four percent. If you believe in mix shift, you are watching a thin-margin intermediary turn, one quarter at a time, into a brand house. The balance sheet has also been repaired, with borrowings down to ₹194 Cr and a small net cash position. A supporter who stopped there would be right about every number.

Now the best case against, and I want you to hear it from the company itself. On the 29 October call, Ajit Thakur, the CFO, was asked whether 45 days of net working capital could be treated as a steady state. He answered: 'But always this is not sustainable to come to the level where we have to maintain this kind of level. So that would be in the normal range of around 50 days or 52 days that is the number what we are looking at.' Read that sentence twice. The manager of the company's cash is telling you that the very number that produced ₹351 Cr of operating cash flow in six months is below normal. About 84% of that inflow came from a net release of working capital, with suppliers and customers funding the business, not from earnings.

How should you weigh a company that is good against a price that is high? Here is the arithmetic I use, and none of it needs a spreadsheet. On 31 March the stock cost 12.9 times the profit of the year just ended. Today it costs 30.7 times the profit of the last twelve months. The price rose 176%, while trailing earnings rose about 16%. That means the multiple itself grew 2.4 times while earnings grew 1.16 times: most of the gain is the market paying more for each rupee of profit, not the company earning more. A re-rating like that can be earned by evidence, and some of it was, but it is also exactly the part of a gain that reverses fastest when evidence disappoints.

Let me show you the three outcomes as a story, not a table. In the good outcome, which I give about one chance in five, working capital holds near 50 days, Honeywell renews on current terms, the brand share passes 20%, and FY28 profit per share reaches ₹93.90. At 25 times, that is ₹2,347, a gain of 61%. In the middle outcome, half the probability, sales grow, margins hold around 4.5%, working capital drifts to the 52 to 55 days the CFO himself expects, and profit per share is ₹64.38. At 21 times, which is the blend of a 13x distributor and a 25x brand house, that is ₹1,352, which is 7% below today's price. In the bad outcome, three chances in ten, part of the payables inflow reverses, the licence costs more, and the multiple falls to a distributor's 14 times on ₹33.73 of earnings: ₹472.

Add those up with their weights and you get ₹1,287, which is 11.7% below the close. I want to be fair about what that says and does not say. It does not say the company will fail; the bad outcome still earns ₹50 Cr after interest. It says that the price already pays for the middle outcome and a bit more, so a buyer today is being asked to hope for the top 20% while carrying the whole risk of the bottom 30%. Ketan Patel, the chairman, gave a useful warning on that same call: 'You should not be overconfident and then you should also see a circumstances right from 2000 GST to demonetization to COVID, to the Ukraine war to the Gulf war, something keeps happening, right?' That is the voice of a man who has run this business for thirty years, and it is the right instinct for an investor too.

Why not simply wait for the pullback? That is the question every careful investor asks, and it deserves a straight answer. The technical support band sits between ₹1,184 and ₹1,298, which is 11% to 19% below the close. If the stock came back there, you would be buying at 25 to 27 times trailing profit with the same business risks, and our base case, ₹1,352, would be only 4% above the top of the band. Risking ₹384 to the stop for a reward of ₹54 is a bet you should decline. The price that would pay you properly for the risk is about ₹1,089 on our numbers, where the base case clears 1.5 to 1, and that is a different conversation from buying a pullback.

Let me give you the three horizons in plain terms. For the next three months, a trader has no edge, because the stock has risen 36% in a month while volume has faded to a third of its average; that is a market that is tired, not a market that is accumulating. Over the next eighteen months, the calendar is crowded: a shareholder meeting on 28 November approving shares for the Zicom SaaS purchase, Q3 results in February, and the Honeywell renewal in March. Each can surprise in either direction, but at 30.7 times earnings the good surprises are expected and the bad ones are not. Over five years the business could still be a real compounder, and I would not call it a stay-away; it simply has to prove the cash before it earns the multiple.

I should also tell you how the long-term arithmetic looks if management does what it says. Suppose Creative reaches our weighted FY29 revenue of about ₹5,280 Cr at a 4.55% EBITDA margin. Profit per share lands near ₹89. At 20 times that is ₹1,785, which is a gain of roughly 7% a year from today's price, below what you should demand for the risks in Chapter 6. If instead management delivers its full ₹6,000 Cr at a 5.25% margin, profit per share is about ₹126 and the stock at 20 times is worth ₹2,525, a 20% annual return. The lesson is that you are paying today for something close to the top of the range of outcomes, and that is not where I like to put new money.

So what do I tell you to do? For new capital, the verdict is REJECTED, and I mean the word. I did not write 'wait for support' because support would not fix the arithmetic. For your existing portfolio, there is nothing to decide, because the positions ledger shows you do not own a single share of Creative Newtech, so no hold, trim or exit action applies and zero shares are to be sold. For the cash itself, I looked at two names on the active shortlist and two outside, and none clears its own entry condition today: AJMERA and MANORAMA are a hair above their support bands, Redington is in a Stage 3 pullback with reward-to-risk under one, and Rashi is in a downtrend. Cash is not a failure of imagination; it is the position that wins when nothing clears the bar.

What would change my mind, and when will we know? I gave you four triggers in the table. The first is a price at or below about ₹1,089, with the stop at ₹913.79, which would make the base case worth 1.5 times the risk. The second is the Q3 FY27 result in February: net working capital between 52 and 55 days and nine-month operating cash flow of at least half of profit would tell us the H1 inflow was structural. The third is clarity on the Honeywell renewal in March 2027. The fourth is the 28 November vote and the final price at which new shares are issued for Zicom, without a larger equity raise behind it. If three of those four arrive, I would re-underwrite this stock from scratch, and I would not be embarrassed to change the verdict.

Let me close with the lesson that I think matters most for you beyond this one stock. A distributor is a business that is easy to grow and hard to finance. Growth shows up in the profit and loss account within a quarter; the cost of that growth shows up in the cash-flow statement and the balance sheet, often a year later and in someone else's ledger. Creative Newtech has done the first part exceptionally well and has begun to prove the second. A disciplined investor does not need to pretend the first half of that sentence is wrong in order to decline to pay for the second half in advance.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Good companies are not the same thing as good purchases. The whole discipline of this chapter is separating the two. Creative Newtech earns a conditional pass on business quality, and that is a respectable finding for a distributor. But a conditional business deserves a price that pays for the condition, and at ₹1,458.40 the price pays for the best version of it. Declining is not pessimism about the company; it is respect for the arithmetic.

book_callouts.title: THE ASYMMETRY TEST IN ONE LINE
book_callouts.text: Ask how much you could make if the base case happens, divide it by how much you could lose if the stop is hit, and require at least 1.5. For Creative Newtech from the top of the support zone, that is ₹54 of reward for ₹384 of risk: 0.14 to 1.
